Empirical Research Plan – Elite Exam Schools in Boston & NYC
----------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy
   • Method: Sharp or (if admissions are not perfectly deterministic) fuzzy Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) around the admission‐score cutoffs.  
   • Rationale:  
     – Assignment to an exam school is a deterministic (or nearly deterministic) step‐function of a continuous running variable – the entrance‐exam composite score.  
     – Within a narrow window around each cohort/ school’s cutoff, students who score just above and just below are plausibly comparable on all unobservables; the cutoff creates quasi-random assignment.  
     – The administrative files contain precise scores and the actual admission decision, allowing classical RDD implementation plus a fuzzy 2SLS when take-up is imperfect.

2. Treatment and Control
   • Treatment variable  
     Treated = 1 if student **enrolls** in an exam school for 9th grade (or 7th grade for NYC), 0 otherwise.  
   • Control group  
     Students who applied but **just missed** the cutoff and therefore enroll in their regular public high school (or another non-exam alternative).  
   • Timing / variation  
     The forcing variable is the exam score relative to the cutoff in the application year. We estimate local average treatment effects (LATE) at each cutoff and pool across cohorts/schools.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
   1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff (no other discrete changes at the score threshold). Plausible: the test is standardized; nothing else besides admission changes discontinuously with the score.  
   2. No precise manipulation of exam scores. Plausible: tests are proctored and externally graded; students cannot finely target a specific score. We will test for density jumps (McCrary test).  
   3. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers exactly at the margin). Some peer interactions across neighborhoods could violate this but are likely small locally.  
   4. First-stage relevance (for fuzzy RD): Crossing the cutoff strongly increases enrollment probability. Clearly satisfied in historical admissions data (>80 p.p. jump).  
   5. Common support / overlap around the cutoff within chosen bandwidths. Administrative data are dense enough to fulfill this.

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
   a. Sorting / score manipulation  
      – Perform McCrary density test and bunching graphics.  
      – If manipulation is detected, use “donut RD” dropping ±1–2 score points near the cutoff.  
   b. Differential attrition or missing post-treatment test scores  
      – Balance checks on attrition rates.  
      – Use inverse probability weighting or Lee bounds if attrition differs.  
   c. Heterogeneous cutoffs & multiple running variables (score + ranked school choices)  
      – Estimate separate RDs for each school-cutoff-cohort, then aggregate via fixed effects / meta-analysis.  
      – Use fuzzy RD with an instrument equal to “above cutoff for first chosen exam school.”

5. R Code Outline
```r
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(rdrobust)   # non-parametric RD
library(ivreg)      # 2SLS for fuzzy RD
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
bny <- read_csv("examSchoolApplicants_BOS_NYC.csv")

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct core variables
bny <- bny %>% 
  mutate(
    running   = exam_score - cutoff_score,      # score distance
    treat_iv  = if_else(running >= 0, 1, 0),    # instrument: above cutoff
    enrolled  = if_else(enrolled_exam == 1, 1, 0),  # actual take-up
    # outcome example: 10th-grade math z-score
    y_math10  = scale(math_grade10_raw)         
  )

# Keep students within ±30 points (bandwidth pre-choice)
bny_local <- bny %>% filter(abs(running) <= 30)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main specification – fuzzy RD (local Wald / 2SLS)
# Non-parametric rdrobust
rd_fuzzy <- rdrobust(y = bny_local$y_math10,
                     x = bny_local$running,
                     c = 0,
                     fuzzy = bny_local$enrolled)

summary(rd_fuzzy)

# Equivalent local 2SLS with polynomial controls
bny_local <- bny_local %>%
  mutate(poly1 = running,
         poly2 = running^2)

mod_2sls <- ivreg(y_math10 ~ enrolled + poly1 + poly2 |
                               treat_iv + poly1 + poly2,
                  data = bny_local)
summary(mod_2sls)

# ------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Robustness – bandwidth sensitivity loop
for (bw in c(10,15,20,25,30)) {
  tmp <- bny %>% filter(abs(running) <= bw)
  cat("\nBandwidth =", bw, "\n")
  print(rdrobust(y = tmp$y_math10,
                 x = tmp$running,
                 fuzzy = tmp$enrolled)$tau_hat)
}

# Additional robustness: McCrary test
library(rddensity)
rddensity(bny$running)$test
```

6. Expected Results
   • Direction: Ambiguous. Peer effects (better peers) push up achievement, but larger within-school competition and curriculum pacing could offset gains. Prior empirical evidence suggests **zero to small positive** impacts (≈ 0–0.10 SD) on standardized scores.  
   • Magnitude: I would expect at most +0.05 SD in math and ELA within two years, possibly negligible longer-run.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)
   • No manipulation of running variable ………………… 0.8  
   • Continuity of covariates at cutoff …………………… 1.0  
   • Strong first stage (fuzzy) ……………………………… 1.0  
   • Low attrition / balanced missingness ……………… 0.6  
   • Appropriate bandwidth & specification choices …… 0.9  

   Overall internal validity ≈ 0.86 – credible local causal effects but external validity limited to applicants near the margin.
